Title: What Your Agents Need to Know About Software Delivery
Abstract:
**[Harness free plan - sign up here!](https://app.harness.io/auth/#/signup?utm_source=webinar&utm_medium=webinar&utm_campaign=2026q4-conf42-mlops)**

Before a coding agent changes a service, it helps to know who owns it, where it runs, and what shipped last week. A pipeline agent preparing to promote that same service needs a different answer. Are there open incidents? Does the artifact it’s about to deploy have a critical vulnerability? Both agents need to know how the code, the artifact, and the running service relate to one another.

We’ll show how Harness models those relationships in a software delivery knowledge graph and makes them available to agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). We’ll follow a plain-language question from prompt to answer, showing how the graph checks that the requested relationships exist and returns only the records the user has permission to see.


In the demo, we’ll ask a coding agent the same question with and without the graph. You’ll see which details it can establish from the repository alone and what it can verify once it can follow a change into production.


Thanks!

Title: Running 50+ AI agents in production: the patterns that held up
Abstract:
I build and run a platform of 50+ Claude agents on Amazon Bedrock at Ruby, a US AI startup. They research companies and the people in them, and write briefings before sales calls, for real customers every day.

Getting the first agent working was the easy part. This talk is about what comes next: keeping dozens of agents accurate, measurable and affordable once real traffic arrives.

What I'll cover, with real traces and numbers:

- Let the AI suggest, let the code decide. Scores, formatting and anything that changes a customer's data stay in normal code. It's cheaper, and you can actually test it.
- Know when quality drops. Quick code checks on every run, and AI judges on a sample of about 1,500 runs a month. One lesson: a judge that can't see what the agent saw will mark correct answers as wrong. Giving it the tool results took one answer from 0.2 to 0.95.
- Keep the bill under control. We cut our cost per run by about 75%. A big part was prompt caching, which also breaks without any error: a date in the system prompt or tools in a different order is enough. I'll show how to catch it, including a limit I measured on live Bedrock.
- Make it fast. Running independent agents in parallel cut the time to research a company from about 32 minutes to 11.

You'll leave with a short checklist you can use on your own agents the next day.

Title: Your Agent Failed Mid-Run. Logs Won't Replay It.
Abstract:
In production, a multi-step agent can fail mid-run: a bad tool call, a wrong intermediate answer, a broken handoff. Logs usually confirm that something broke. They rarely give you the run back so you can inspect the exact step and try another path. The usual next move is to re-run everything: more time, more tokens, and the same live side effects again.

This talk is about a practical habit for that failure mode: record → replay → fork. Save the full agent run as a local cassette (e.g. prompts, tool calls, and results). Replay the same steps to find where it went wrong. Fork from that step with a fix, and check it before you re-run in production.

Demo: a failed multi-step agent run. We rewind to the bad step, fork a fix, and show recovery without re-running the whole pipeline. Traces help you observe; a cassette lets you reproduce the run and change one decision. Flashback is one way to keep those cassettes. The talk teaches the habit, not a product pitch.

You leave with: how to treat a failed agent run like a replayable artifact next to logs, traces, and re-runs.

Title: From 173 Billion Documents to Training Data: A Beginner's Tour of LLM Data Processing
Abstract:
A model learns everything it knows from its training data. Where does that data come from, and what makes text suitable? This talk answers both questions based on our work at Fraunhofer IAIS.

The running example is OpenGPT-X, the project that produced the open Teuken models. I follow its data from a raw Common Crawl dump to a clean, deduplicated corpus: what curated sources and web crawls each give you, why metadata normalization matters, how filtering removes 96.94% of web documents (and why that is the pipeline doing its job), and why deduplication consumes 80% of the compute budget.

Every claim comes with an honest number, from CPU hours to euros per document. By the end you will know how a training corpus is built, and what that tells you about the models trained on it. No data-pipeline experience needed.

Title: Research to Reliable ML: Lessons from a Deep Learning Pipeline for Skin Lesion Classification
Abstract:
Building a machine learning model that performs well in an experiment is only one part of developing a reliable ML system. Reproducibility, data quality, evaluation methodology and deployment readiness are equally important, particularly in healthcare applications where model predictions could eventually inform clinical decisions.

In this talk, I will use my research on deep learning for skin lesion classification as a case study to explore the practical considerations involved in developing an end-to-end medical imaging workflow. My work combines U-Net segmentation with CNN architectures, including ResNet50, VGG16 and EfficientNetB4, and achieved a reported AUC of 0.99 on the evaluated PH² dataset.

I will discuss the challenges of structuring image-processing and classification workflows, maintaining consistency across preprocessing and evaluation, interpreting performance metrics, and recognising the limitations of results obtained from a single dataset. I will also examine what would be needed to move from an experimental research pipeline towards a more reproducible, monitored and deployment-ready ML system, including versioned data and models, automated testing, experiment tracking and independent validation.

Using this case study, I aim to demonstrate why reliable machine learning requires more than selecting an architecture and achieving a strong metric. It requires a systematic approach to the entire lifecycle, from data preparation and experimentation to validation, monitoring and maintenance.

Title: Agent Evals That Check What Actually Happened
Abstract:
A better answer score does not prove that an AI agent completed its task. Learn how to evaluate tool-using agents through observable actions and outcomes, and turn those checks into release decisions for code, prompt and model changes.

An agent can produce a convincing completion message while a tool request remains unresolved, an action has been repeated, or a required approval was missing. A text-only evaluation can reward the response while overlooking the execution failure. Conversely, an agent that refuses every action is not a reliable system simply because it avoids unsafe effects.

Drawing on Sajal Garg's work on automated LLM evaluation infrastructure at Microsoft AI, this session develops an evaluation workflow around a non-confidential illustrative task. It separates deterministic checks on actions and service state from quality judgments on generated content, distinguishes infrastructure and judge failures from task failures, and uses controlled interruption and lost-acknowledgement cases to test recovery. It also explains why test state must be reset and variable behavior evaluated across repeated runs.

The closing section connects the results to regression gates: compare current and candidate versions on the same cases, preserve the versioned inputs and checks, and keep critical execution failures separate from aggregate quality scores. Attendees leave with a failure taxonomy, concrete action/effect assertions and a practical agent-evaluation release checklist. This is an operational evaluation session, not a worker-pool architecture talk or product demonstration.

Title: Compliance as a Pipeline Stage: Automating AI Governance in MLOps
Abstract:
Most ML teams treat compliance as a review that happens before launch. Under the EU AI Act, U.S. AI governance frameworks, and privacy laws, that approach breaks down, because models are retrained, redeployed, and updated continuously.

This talk shows how to move governance into the MLOps pipeline itself. Drawing on experience building automated GDPR compliance systems, ROPA reporting pipelines, and data governance platforms at Meta, Arpita covers:

- Risk classification at model registration
- Lineage capture across datasets, features, and model versions
- Policy checks as CI/CD gates before training and deployment
- Monitoring signals that feed compliance evidence
- Documentation generated automatically from pipeline metadata

The talk also covers practical trade-offs, including where automated gates slow teams down and how to keep engineering and compliance aligned without manual handoffs.

Title: Shipping Agentic AI to Production: What a Regulated Enterprise Learned the Hard Way
Abstract: A practitioner talk on moving agentic AI from demos to production in a regulated enterprise: per-agent identity and least-privilege access, risk-adaptive policy gates that auto-approve low-risk actions and escalate high-risk ones, immutable audit, and evaluation as a platform-enforced MLOps gate — grounded in public agent benchmarks and production failure patterns, plus 20 years of platform work including a 20,000-pipeline migration. Takeaway: a reference pattern — identity, scoped grant, policy gate, audit — and a checklist for operating agents in production.

Title: Self-Signed Evidence: Why Your LLM Agent's Green Checks Prove Nothing
Abstract:
An LLM support agent finds two orders for the same blender, picks one and calls the refund tool. Code confirms the order is the customer's, recent and under the limit, then pays. The broken blender was in the other order.

Putting the check in code did not help: it trusted an order ID the model chose. I call this self-signed evidence.

I build LLM agents that spend customers' money. In public τ²-bench runs I counted 82 of 1,632 conversations where tools accepted a change to an order the task never asked to change; in at least 21, the model picked the order itself.

You will learn to find the model-written values your checks trust, test a check with a swapped order ID, and run it in shadow before it is allowed to block. For engineers whose agents issue refunds or make bookings.

Title: Edge MLOps: Building a Pipeline from PyTorch Training to On-Device Inference with ExecuTorch
Abstract:
Most MLOps pipelines end at a cloud endpoint. When the target is a phone, the pipeline has to account for memory limits, thermal budgets, battery drain, and a fleet of devices with very different hardware. Drawing on contributions to Meta's open-source PyTorch ExecuTorch runtime, this talk walks through what an edge-focused MLOps pipeline needs:

- Exporting PyTorch models into a mobile runtime built on a model loader, execution planner, memory manager, and operator registry
- Making compression part of the pipeline: quantization-aware training, structured pruning, and knowledge distillation
- Why quantization-aware training preserves accuracy better than post-training quantization alone
- Validating models across device tiers, including NPU versus CPU execution paths
- Fitting models within binary-size and thermal constraints before release

Attendees leave with a reference pipeline for taking models from training to production on consumer mobile devices.

Title: Coding Noisy Product Names for Consumer Price Statistics: Trie Rules, Bag-of-Words and Reliability-Weighted Labeling
Abstract:
We ran a 1D-CNN, an LSTM and a character n-gram logistic regression head to head on the same noisy-product-name task, under one matched training protocol. The logistic regression won every category. This talk is about why, and about what that means for anyone classifying short, messy text.

The setting is consumer price measurement from alternative data: scanner exports, web-scraped listings, transaction and receipt records. They promise broader coverage, and they arrive as short, abbreviated, inconsistently spelled product names with no standard product code. Before any price can be compared, every item has to be mapped to a consumption classification such as COICOP. The method has separately been deployed in production on data that cannot be released; everything measured in this talk comes from the public benchmark.

I will go through the pipeline step by step: domain-specific normalization and tokenization of noisy item names, a prefix-tree (trie) pre-classifier driven by per-category key phrases and stop phrases, and a per-category binary confirmation model that decides whether an item really belongs to the category the rules assigned. I will explain why binary confirmation per category beats one multiclass model here, and what that choice costs you.

One operational lesson worth the ticket on its own: rules look like they are solving the problem, and then they are not. They cover only 32 to 50 percent of items, and coverage erodes as new product names appear. The learned stage is permanent infrastructure, not a stopgap you remove once the rule set matures.

Labels are the other half. The protocol has several annotators giving a binary valid/reject judgment, with votes aggregated by a reliability weight that updates as annotation proceeds. The model sits inside the same rule, so fine-tuning is continual rather than a periodic project. Around 66 labeled examples per category turn out to be enough.

Then the numbers: mean F1 0.997 for the character n-gram logistic regression, word-order features adding nothing, the neural baselines behind. The benchmark is synthetic and public, and I will say plainly what that does and does not establish.

Takeaways: where the bottleneck in noisy short-text classification actually sits, how to structure annotation so it compounds instead of decaying, and how to recognize the case where reaching for a larger, order-sensitive model is the wrong move.

Method, benchmark and reproducibility package: arXiv:2606.02004

Title: Building Resilient MLOps Pipelines for Illiquid Loan Portfolio Valuation
Abstract:
Financial institutions rely on complex models to value mortgages, commercial loans, and other illiquid lending assets under changing market conditions. Moving these models into reliable production environments requires more than accurate calculations—it requires scalable pipelines, reproducibility, observability, and strong controls around data and model changes.

This session presents a practical MLOps architecture for building and operating resilient loan portfolio valuation systems. It explores how market data ingestion, configurable economic scenarios, prepayment assumptions, cash-flow models, and discounting workflows can be organized into repeatable valuation pipelines. The session examines versioning of data, model configurations, and assumptions so teams can reproduce historical valuations, investigate unexpected results, and safely introduce model updates.

The session also covers operational considerations including automated testing, pipeline monitoring, data lineage, failure handling, model validation, and auditability. Event-driven processing patterns are explored as a way to respond efficiently to changes in market data and portfolio positions while supporting scalable computation. Attendees will learn practical architectural principles for transforming financial valuation models into maintainable production systems where reliability, traceability, and reproducibility are treated as core MLOps requirements.

Title: Engineering Cloud Infrastructure for Agentic AI: MLOps and Self-Healing Systems
Abstract:
Agentic AI is reshaping how cloud infrastructure is designed, deployed, and operated. As autonomous systems increasingly perceive, reason, and act, traditional cloud architectures face challenges in managing unpredictable workloads, low-latency requirements, and dynamic resource demands. This session explores practical architectural approaches to building scalable, reliable, and adaptive infrastructure for agentic AI through MLOps principles.

The talk examines how Kubernetes, multi-cloud environments, and orchestration frameworks such as LangChain can support agentic AI workloads. It highlights architectural considerations for resource scaling, workload orchestration, infrastructure automation, and operational efficiency.

A key focus is self-healing cloud operations, where collaborative AI agents can assist with incident detection, automated remediation, and system recovery. The session also explores observability and automation maturity gaps that affect reliability, performance, and service-level objectives.

Attendees will gain insights into designing agentic AI infrastructure with security, governance, compliance, and cost optimization in mind, along with practical considerations for integrating autonomous operations into existing cloud environments.

Title: Scaling Microservices Observability with Agentic LLMs
Abstract:
Modern microservices generate massive volumes of logs, metrics, and distributed traces, making incident detection, root cause analysis, and service reliability increasingly challenging. Traditional observability tools often struggle to correlate signals across complex service dependencies, resulting in delayed investigations and operational blind spots.

This session explores how Agentic Large Language Models (LLMs) can enhance cloud-native observability through semantic analysis, intelligent telemetry correlation, automated causal reasoning, and closed-loop remediation.

Focusing on architecture and operational practices, the presentation examines approaches to integrating LLM-driven analysis into existing observability workflows. Drawing on published research and industry findings, it discusses improvements in event correlation, service dependency mapping, alert accuracy, and incident response, including reductions in Mean Time to Detection (MTTD) and Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR).

Attendees will gain insights into scalability, performance optimization, debugging, security, data privacy, and governance considerations. The session highlights practical approaches to improving observability, automating incident response, and maintaining resilient distributed systems at scale.

Title: Build ML Workflows with Codex, Flyte, and MCP
Abstract:
AI coding tools can write ML code, but reliable execution still needs orchestration. This talk shows how to connect Codex to Flyte through MCP for a reproducible training or evaluation workflow.

I will talk about how OpenAI hosts Flyte for internal training, and how we developed MCP for integration with Codex.

Attendees will leave with a practical workflow pattern and a checklist for debugging, reproducibility, and safe execution.

Title: From Prototype to Millions of Daily Renders: Shipping LLM-Powered Features Reliably at E-commerce Scale
Abstract:
Getting an LLM-powered feature to work in a demo is easy. Serving it on a high-traffic e-commerce page millions of times a day, without hurting latency or showing customers a bad answer, is a different job.

Drawing on shipping AI shopping features at Amazon that reached millions of daily page renders with zero faults, this talk covers the operational side of putting generative AI on a critical page:

- Deciding when content should be generated in real time and when it can be precomputed
- Latency budgets, timeouts and fallbacks so the page never waits on a model
- Quality gates and monitoring that catch bad output before customers see it
- Integrating with an existing AI assistant's orchestration without becoming its bottleneck
- Launching safely: gradual dial-ups, kill switches and the metrics that matter

Attendees leave with a practical checklist for taking an LLM feature from prototype to production traffic.

Title: From PoC to Production: Deploying Agentic AI at Enterprise Scale
Abstract: Most agentic AI demos never survive contact with production. Brittle prompts, no evaluation harness, no guardrails, no ownership model, and the prototype quietly dies after the demo. This case study walks through taking an agentic AI system from prototype to a production deployment serving merchants across more than 600 retail locations. It covers the architecture (multi-agent orchestration for assortment planning and optimization), the evaluation and data-contract testing that run in CI, the default-deny data governance layer, monitoring and cost/latency tradeoffs in production, and the failure modes that only appear at scale. Attendees leave with a concrete checklist for moving their own agent prototypes into production: what to instrument first, which gates actually caught bugs, and the organizational changes (ownership, on-call, stakeholder trust) that mattered as much as the technology.

Title: Defending the AI Factory: Practical Security Strategies for MLOps
Abstract:
As machine learning models transition from experimental notebooks into critical production systems, they become primary targets for sophisticated cyberattacks. Standard DevOps security is no longer enough to protect the unique components of the machine learning lifecycle.

This intermediate-level talk dives deep into SecMLOps (Security in Machine Learning Operations), exploring how vulnerabilities manifest across the entire ML pipeline. Attendees will learn how to secure data ingestion pipelines against data poisoning, protect model registries from unauthorized tampering, mitigate supply chain risks in Python dependencies, and defend deployed endpoints against adversarial and extraction attacks. Through real-world architectural patterns and practical toolchains, this session provides actionable strategies to build resilient, secure, and compliant AI systems without stalling developer velocity.

Title: Securing the AI Stack: From Models to Agents to Infrastructure
Abstract:
Training the model is the easy part. Shipping an AI system you'd trust with real data, real tools, and real actions is where teams stall, usually because nobody has a map of where the risks actually live.

In this lightning talk, I'll give you that map: a four-layer defense-in-depth framework for production AI, with the one threat and one fix that matter most at each layer.

- Model: indirect prompt injection. Fix: validate every output before it drives an action.
- Agents: over-permissioned agents. Fix: tool allowlists and approval gates for irreversible actions.
- Tools and MCP: poisoned or unvetted tool servers. Fix: allowlist, schema-validate, and pin them like dependencies.
- Infrastructure: poisoned weights and silent exfiltration. Fix: scan models in CI/CD and restrict egress.

Every layer has holes, but stacked together they leave no straight path from attacker to impact.

You'll leave with a 16-question checklist, four per layer, that you can run against your own pipeline this sprint.

Title: Who Is Calling Your Model? Identity and Authorization for AI Agents and ML Pipelines
Abstract:
Your ML platform is full of non-human actors: training jobs pulling data, inference services calling feature stores, CI pipelines pushing models, and now AI agents calling tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) on behalf of real users. Most of them authenticate with shared API keys or over-privileged service accounts, and very few teams can answer: which workload made this call, on whose behalf, and how do I revoke it?

This talk walks through a practical identity architecture for ML and agent systems, based on lessons from building identity products for AI agents:

- Workload identity instead of secrets – giving pipelines, model servers and agents verifiable identities (SPIFFE/SPIRE-style) and short-lived credentials instead of long-lived keys.
- Delegated access for agents – how an agent should get scoped, user-bound access to tools and APIs: OAuth token exchange, MCP authorization, and registering agent clients with Client ID Metadata Documents.
- Guardrails in the loop – where human approval, step-up and revocation belong when agents take real actions.
- What goes wrong – over-scoped tokens, confused-deputy calls between services, invisible agent-to-agent hops, and the missing kill switch, with fixes for each.

You'll leave with a reference architecture and a checklist you can apply to your own ML platform and agent deployments.

Title: Testing Agents for Permission Leaks: Authorization Evals in the Delivery Pipeline
Abstract:
Most agent evaluation suites measure accuracy, helpfulness, and task completion. Few test whether the agent reveals data the current user isn’t allowed to see. In regulated environments, that gap is the one that matters most.

This talk shows how to treat authorization as a testable property of an agent system and run it in the delivery pipeline like any other regression suite. Drawing on experience building multi-agent systems over enterprise banking CRM data, it covers:

- Persona-based test users with different entitlements running the same tasks
- Leak assertions that check responses, summaries, and tool calls for restricted facts
- Combination tests that catch disclosures created when individually permitted results are joined
- Regression triggers for model upgrades, prompt changes, and new tools
- Making failures debuggable by linking each leak to the tool call and context that caused it

Attendees will leave with a blueprint for adding authorization evals to their agent release process.

Title: Fixing Exposure Bias in Production Ranking Systems Through Reliable MLOps Pipelines
Abstract:
Production recommendation systems depend on reliable training data pipelines to deliver accurate and personalized experiences. However, flawed exposure signals can silently introduce bias, distort model learning, and reinforce historically popular content. Addressing these issues requires careful data validation, pipeline improvements, and disciplined model evaluation.

This session presents a practical MLOps case study on identifying and correcting exposure bias in large-scale ranking systems. It explores how traditional server-side tracking incorrectly records unseen content as user exposure, resulting in misleading negative training examples and reduced recommendation diversity.

The presentation examines an engineering approach to replacing inaccurate proxy signals with directly measured exposure data. Key implementation considerations include validating new data sources, running legacy and corrected pipelines in parallel, removing invalid training labels, and adjusting model training strategies. It also discusses offline evaluation, controlled online experimentation, and the trade-offs between recommendation precision and exposure diversity.

Attendees will learn practical techniques for detecting hidden training data issues, improving pipeline reliability, and validating model behavior before production rollout. The session highlights how systematic data quality improvements, evidence-driven experimentation, and cross-team collaboration can strengthen MLOps practices and support more reliable, scalable, and trustworthy recommendation systems in production environments.
